title: Design a distributed message queue (Kafka-like)
scopeHtml: Scope: partitioned log, replication and ISR, producers and consumer groups, delivery semantics, retention. Questions are still to be written.

notes.title: Requirements
notes.html:
A distributed message queue lets producers write messages that consumers read later, decoupling the two. A Kafka-like system is a durable, partitioned, replicated log. LinkedIn built Kafka to move activity events; now Uber, Netflix and most big companies use it as the backbone between services.

Functional

  • Producers publish messages to a topic.
  • Consumers subscribe and read messages; consumer groups share the work.
  • Messages keep their order within a partition; replay from any offset.
  • Retention: keep messages for N days (not deleted on read).

Non-functional

  • Throughput: millions of messages/s across the cluster.
  • Durability: acknowledged messages survive broker failures.
  • Availability: brokers can fail without stopping producers/consumers.
  • Low latency (single-digit ms to tens of ms end to end).
  • Scale by adding brokers and partitions.

Decision gravity. Choosing a log (append-only, offset-based, retained) over a classic queue (delete after ack, as RabbitMQ/SQS) is the root decision: it allows replay and many independent readers, but gives up per-message ack/redelivery and priority. Reversible only at high migration cost; consumers depend on offset semantics.

Everyday analogy. A newspaper archive: publishers add editions to the end; each reader keeps a bookmark and can reread old ones.

Common interview traps.

  • Treating Kafka like RabbitMQ (per-message delete, priorities).
  • Forgetting replay and multiple consumer groups as requirements.
  • Not asking about ordering guarantees.

notes.title: API
notes.html:
Producer

POST /v1/topics/orders/messages        (or client library send())
{ "key": "user-42", "value": "<bytes>", "headers": {"traceId":"abc"},
  "acks": "all", "idempotentProducerId": 7712, "sequence": 1034 }

200 { "partition": 3, "offset": 889112 }
400 -> message too large (default max 1 MB)
503 -> not enough in-sync replicas (NotEnoughReplicas)

Consumer

POST /v1/groups/billing/subscribe   { "topics": ["orders"] }

GET  /v1/groups/billing/poll?maxBytes=1048576&timeoutMs=500
200 { "records": [ {"topic":"orders","partition":3,"offset":889112,
                    "key":"user-42","value":"<b64>"} ] }

POST /v1/groups/billing/commit
{ "offsets": [ {"topic":"orders","partition":3,"offset":889113} ] }

Admin

POST /v1/topics   { "name":"orders", "partitions":24, "replicationFactor":3,
                    "config":{"retention.ms":604800000, "min.insync.replicas":2} }

Real Kafka uses a binary TCP protocol (Produce, Fetch, OffsetCommit, JoinGroup), but the semantics above are the same: producers pick the partition (by key hash), consumers pull and commit offsets.

Industry example. Kafka's acks=all + min.insync.replicas=2 is the standard "do not lose data" setting.

Everyday analogy. The producer drops a letter into numbered mailboxes; readers say "I have read up to letter 889,112".

Common interview traps.

  • A push-based consumer design that overwhelms slow consumers (Kafka pulls for backpressure).
  • Forgetting offsets belong to the consumer group.

notes.title: Estimates
notes.html:
Assume 1M messages/s peak, 1 KB each, retention 7 days, replication factor 3.

Quantity Calculation Result
Ingress 1M x 1 KB 1 GB/s
Replication traffic x2 extra copies 2 GB/s between brokers
Egress (3 consumer groups) 3 x 1 GB/s 3 GB/s
Daily data 1 GB/s x 86,400 ~86 TB/day raw
7-day retention with RF 3 86 TB x 7 x 3 ~1.8 PB (a lot; usually average load is 10x lower)
Brokers (50 MB/s/disk-friendly, say 100 MB/s per broker write incl. replication) 3 GB/s total write / 0.1 ~30 brokers
Partitions per-partition throughput ~10 MB/s (conservative) 1 GB/s / 10 MB/s = 100 partitions min; choose 200 to 600

Use average (say 100k msg/s) for storage: 100 MB/s x 86,400 = 8.6 TB/day, x7 x3 = ~180 TB. Real design sizes disks for average, network for peak.

Partition count rule of thumb: target throughput / per-partition throughput, and at least the max number of consumers you want running in parallel in one group.

Everyday analogy. Estimating how many newspaper printing presses and warehouses you need, given edition size and how long you keep copies.

Common interview traps.

  • Sizing storage for peak instead of average.
  • Forgetting replication multiplies both disk and network.
  • Setting thousands of partitions per topic "to be safe" (costs memory, open files, election time).

notes.title: High-level design
notes.html:
Components

  • Broker: a server holding partition logs on disk.
  • Topic -> partitions: each partition is an ordered, append-only log; the unit of parallelism and ordering.
  • Replication: each partition has a leader and followers; followers copy the leader. Reads and writes go to the leader.
  • Controller / metadata quorum: elects leaders and tracks cluster state (ZooKeeper historically, KRaft in Kafka 3.x onward).
  • Consumer groups: each partition is consumed by exactly one consumer within a group; groups are independent.
  • Producers choose partition by hash(key) % partitions (same key goes to the same partition, preserving per-key order).

Decision gravity. Partition count is nearly a one-way door: you can increase it, but doing so changes hash(key) % n and breaks key-to-partition ordering for existing keys; decreasing it requires a new topic. Replication factor 3 is a deliberate cost for durability; RF=1 is reversible but loses data on a disk failure.

Industry examples. LinkedIn runs trillions of messages/day on Kafka; Uber built tiering and federation on top; Confluent, MSK and Redpanda offer managed or compatible versions. Pulsar separates compute (brokers) from storage (BookKeeper) as an alternative.

Everyday analogy. A post office with many numbered sorting lanes; each lane has one clerk (leader) and two backups.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing a topic as a whole is ordered (only each partition is).
  • Having more consumers than partitions and expecting more parallelism (extras sit idle).

notes.title: Deep dives
notes.html:
Why a log is fast: sequential disk and zero copy

Each partition is a directory of segment files (for example 1 GB each) named by their first offset, plus an index (offset to file position). Writes only append, and sequential disk I/O is fast (hundreds of MB/s on HDD, GB/s on SSD). Kafka relies on the OS page cache instead of its own cache and uses sendfile (zero copy) to move bytes from page cache to the network without copying through user space.

partition-3/
  00000000000000000000.log     offsets 0 .. 889,000
  00000000000000000000.index   sparse offset -> byte position
  00000000000000889001.log     active segment (being appended)

Reading from an offset: binary search the segment list by name, then the sparse index, then scan a few KB. Messages are batched and compressed (lz4/zstd) per batch, giving 3x to 5x savings.

Replication, ISR and leader election

  • Followers fetch from the leader like consumers. The set of followers that are caught up is the ISR (in-sync replicas).
  • A message is committed once all ISR members have it; consumers only see committed messages (up to the high-water mark).
  • Producer acks: 0 (fire and forget), 1 (leader only, may lose on leader crash), all (every ISR member).
  • min.insync.replicas=2 with RF=3: if ISR shrinks below 2, writes fail rather than risk loss (safety over availability).
  • Leader dies: the controller picks a new leader from the ISR, so no committed message is lost. unclean.leader.election.enable=false prevents electing an out-of-sync replica (which would lose data).

Worked example. RF=3, acks=all, min.insync.replicas=2: can lose any 1 broker with no data loss and no downtime; losing 2 brokers stops writes to affected partitions but keeps committed data.

Decision gravity. acks=all costs ~1 extra network round trip (a few ms) for durability; reversible per producer. Allowing unclean election is a deliberate availability-over-consistency choice, risky to flip on later.

Consumer groups and rebalancing

Partitions are assigned among consumers in the group (range, round-robin, or cooperative sticky assignors). Each consumer tracks an offset per partition, committed to an internal topic __consumer_offsets.

When a consumer joins, leaves or misses heartbeats (session.timeout.ms=45000), the group rebalances: partitions are reassigned and, in the old "eager" protocol, all consumers pause. Cooperative rebalancing moves only affected partitions.

Production incident pattern. Symptom: consumer lag grows and stays high, processing pauses in waves. Metric: records-lag-max, rebalance count. Cause: slow processing exceeds max.poll.interval.ms (default 5 min), the broker thinks the consumer died and rebalances repeatedly. Fix: process less per poll (max.poll.records), or increase the interval, or move work to a thread pool.

Delivery semantics

Semantics How Risk
At most once Commit offset before processing Loses messages on crash
At least once Process, then commit Duplicates on crash/retry
Exactly once Idempotent producer + transactions + commit offsets in the same transaction Higher overhead, only within Kafka

Idempotent producer (enable.idempotence=true): each producer has an ID, each message a sequence number per partition; the broker drops duplicates from retries. Transactions write to several partitions and the consumer offsets atomically (used by Kafka Streams). Across external systems (a DB), exactly once means at-least-once plus an idempotent consumer (dedupe by message ID or upsert).

Retention, compaction and ordering

  • Time/size retention: delete whole old segments (retention.ms=7 days, retention.bytes). Cheap: deleting a file.
  • Log compaction: keep only the latest value per key (for changelogs, such as a user profile table). Tombstone (null value) deletes a key.
  • Ordering: guaranteed within a partition. Use a key (for example orderId) so related events land together. Hot key (one huge customer) overloads one partition: add salting or sub-keys if order across them is not needed.
  • Poison messages: a message that always fails; send to a dead letter topic after N retries rather than blocking the partition.

Pull vs push, and backpressure

Consumers pull, so a slow consumer simply lags without overwhelming itself or the broker. Long polling (fetch.max.wait.ms) avoids empty round trips. Push systems (RabbitMQ default) need prefetch limits to avoid flooding.

Beyond one cluster

Cross-region: MirrorMaker 2 or Cluster Linking replicates topics asynchronously. Tiered storage (Kafka 3.6+, early access then production-maturing; confirm in docs) offloads old segments to S3 to cut disk cost.

Everyday analogy. The ISR is the group of backup clerks who have the same ledger as the head clerk; you only announce a letter as "received" when all the up-to-date backups have written it down.

Common interview traps.

  • Claiming exactly-once delivery everywhere; it is only effectively-once with idempotent consumers outside Kafka.
  • Setting acks=1 and being surprised by data loss on leader failure.
  • Not mentioning consumer lag as the key health metric.
  • Adding consumers beyond the partition count.

notes.title: What interviewers look for
notes.html:
• The log abstraction: partitions, offsets, retention, replay, consumer groups.
  • Numbers: throughput, partitions per topic, brokers, replication overhead, retention storage.
  • Replication: leader/follower, ISR, acks, min.insync.replicas, what is lost in each failure.
  • Ordering guarantees (per-partition) and key choice.
  • Delivery semantics and idempotency, with honest limits of exactly-once.
  • Operational thinking: lag monitoring, rebalances, poison messages, hot partitions.
  • Seniors compare Kafka with RabbitMQ/SQS/Pulsar, discuss KRaft replacing ZooKeeper, tiered storage, multi-region replication and schema evolution (Schema Registry, Avro/Protobuf).

Common interview traps.

  • Drawing boxes (broker, ZooKeeper) with no explanation of the log and replication.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Kafka-like = partitioned, replicated, append-only log with retention; consumers pull and track offsets.
  • Partition = unit of ordering and parallelism; key hash picks it; partition count is hard to change safely.
  • Speed comes from sequential I/O, batching, compression, page cache and zero-copy.
  • Durability: RF=3, acks=all, min.insync.replicas=2, no unclean election; committed data survives one broker loss.
  • Consumer groups share partitions; rebalances and lag are the main operational pain.
  • At-least-once plus idempotent consumers is the practical default; exactly-once needs idempotent producer and transactions.
  • The log-vs-queue choice and partition count are the near one-way doors.
